title: Brojevi i kahva
reviewerNotes: Full draft to Lesson 1 exemplar bar. ready for human review before publish.
storyBeat: Amira’s café becomes HQ; Ana learns numbers 1. 20 and orders kahva while Mrvica steals the scene.

vocabulary: Café words: kahva, fildžan, lokum, molim
grammar: Koliko? for how many / how much
culture: Time, copper tray, and not rushing the cup

grammar.title: Numbers 1. 20
grammar.explanation: Learn 1. 10 cold, then 11. 20 as a chant. 1 jedan, 2 dva, 3 tri, 4 četiri, 5 pet, 6 šest, 7 sedam, 8 osam, 9 devet, 10 deset. Then: 11 jedanaest, 12 dvanaest, 13 trinaest, 14 četrnaest, 15 petnaest, 16 šesnaest, 17 sedamnaest, 18 osamnaest, 19 devetnaest, 20 dvadeset. Notice četiri and šest need accents when you type.

grammar.title: Koliko?
grammar.explanation: Koliko? asks how many or how much. At a café you will hear Koliko košta? (How much does it cost?) and Koliko fildžana? (How many cups?). Answer with a number: Dva. / Deset KM. Keep it short.

grammar.title: Ordering coffee. say it as a chunk
grammar.explanation: For now, order with ready-made lines. Kahvu, molim means “Coffee, please” (kahvu is the form you hear when ordering). Jednu kahvu, molim = one coffee please. Dva fildžana, molim = two cups please. Do not worry about full case charts yet. memorize the café lines.

culture.title: Kahva at Amira’s. slow on purpose
culture.body: Bosnian coffee arrives in a džezva on a copper tray, with a small fildžan and often lokum. You pour, wait a moment for the grounds to settle, and talk. Rushing the cup is missing the point. Amira’s café becomes Ana and Emir’s HQ: Mrvica patrols the chairs and occasionally steals the scene.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A: Count to twenty
lessonBlocks.body: Say 1. 10 slowly, then faster: jedan dva tri četiri pet šest sedam osam devet deset. include the special letter for četiri and šest. Next chant 11. 20: jedanaest, dvanaest, trinaest, četrnaest, petnaest, šesnaest, sedamnaest, osamnaest, devetnaest, dvadeset. Point at fingers, pigeons, or lokum pieces and count aloud. Ana drills numbers while Emir checks the time. petnaest minuta to Amira’s.
tips: četiri and šest need accents when typing

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B: Order at Amira’s
lessonBlocks.body: Walk in with Zdravo! or Dobar dan! Order: Kahvu, molim. or Jednu kahvu, molim. If Emir joins: Dva fildžana, molim. Ask Koliko košta? if you want the price. Add Hvala when the tray arrives. If Amira offers lokum, smile and say Hvala. Mrvica may appear: Ana can say Zdravo, Mrvica! without new grammar. Numbers + molim + kahva are enough for your first café win.
tips: Order kit: Kahvu, molim · Dva fildžana, molim · Koliko košta?

funFacts.title: kahva with an h
funFacts.body: In much of Bosnia and Herzegovina you will hear and see kahva. Related standards nearby may prefer kava or kafa. This course stays with the Bosnian café form you meet at Amira’s. Spell it with the h so your notebook matches the tray in front of you.

funFacts.title: Fildžan is tiny on purpose
funFacts.body: A fildžan is small because the coffee ritual is meant to last. You sip, talk, and pour again from the džezva. Quantity is not the point of Bosnian coffee service. Company is the point, and the tiny cup keeps you at the table.

funFacts.title: Lokum on the tray
funFacts.body: Sweet lokum often arrives with Bosnian coffee. Saying yes to one piece is friendly and normal. Eating the whole plate without asking is bold. Treat lokum as part of the coffee welcome, not a free dessert challenge.

funFacts.title: Mrvica means little crumb
funFacts.body: Mrvica literally points to a little crumb. It is a fitting name for a café cat who believes every table is hers. She appears whenever sugar, lokum, or attention is available. In this course, her name is both vocabulary and a warning about unattended snacks.

civicContext.title: A currency without normal monetary freedom
civicContext.body: Daily life in Bosnia and Herzegovina runs on a currency system that limits national monetary freedom by design. The convertible mark is managed through a currency-board arrangement tied to the euro. That setup helps keep prices more stable, but it also means the state cannot run flexible monetary policy the way many countries do. Café prices and wages therefore sit inside a postwar economic structure that traded policy freedom for stability.
